claims.text: Independent Monte Carlo simulations can accurately decouple lattice and electronic heat transport in HfNbTaTiZr.
Electronic heat conduction dominates in HfNbTaTiZr below approximately 200 K.
Phonon heat conduction predominates in HfNbTaTiZr above 300 K.
The model will predict total thermal conductivity within ±10% of experimental values.
Pristine and 1 wt.% oxygen-doped specimens represent realistic defect distributions associated with typical as-cast processing and oxidation states.
Local defects and oxygen impurities modify the local vibrational spectra of HfNbTaTiZr.
Local defects and oxygen impurities modify electronic scattering rates in HfNbTaTiZr.
Sensitivity analysis of electron–phonon coupling can ensure that independently simulated electronic and phononic contributions remain additive.
Separating electron and phonon Monte Carlo chains prevents conflation of lattice and electronic contributions and enables their separate quantification.
Below approximately 200 K, electronic and lattice contributions will be comparably significant.
Above 300 K, phonon conduction will dominate.
The relevant experimental total thermal conductivity is 10–17 W/(K·m).
Earlier approaches relied on Debye-temperature approximations or simplified DFT elasticity models for pristine, defect-free crystals.
Earlier approaches do not capture the complexity of independent electron and phonon transport in real samples.
The predictions are applicable between 100 K and 1200 K when defect distributions are well characterized.
The model will have reduced reliability for extremely inhomogeneous microstructures or outside 100–1200 K.
The estimated ±10% accuracy improvement is based on current experimental data and trends from prior simulations.
Electron–phonon interactions remain challenging to isolate completely.
Modulated laser heating and voltage-noise analysis can separately estimate phonon and electronic thermal-conductivity contributions.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis says electronic conduction dominates below approximately 200 K, whereas the predicted outcome says electronic and lattice contributions are comparably significant in that regime.
The ±10% figure is described both as an absolute agreement/error bound relative to experiment and as an accuracy improvement over prior approaches; these are different performance metrics.
